newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia 97/8 wheat f'cast cut to 16.25 MT.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia 97/8 wheat f'cast cut to 16.25 MT.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) on Tuesday sharply downgraded its forecast for Australia's 1997/98 (July-June) wheat crop to 16.25 million tonnes.

The forecast production cut, from a previous forecast of 19.2 million tonnes, is based on forecasts of dry weather throughout Australia's winter and spring because of an El Nino weather pattern. Australia produced a record 23.59 million tonnes of wheat in 1996/97.
ABARE's latest forecast compares with the Australian Wheat Board's estimate for an 18 million tonne wheat crop.

"With yields well below last season's record, the wheat crop is forecast to be down about 30 percent to 16.25 million tonnes despite plantings being little unchanged," ABARE said in its June quarter Australian Commodities publication.

Crop yields were forecast to be below average in Australia's eastern states reflecting the Bureau of Meteorology's announcement that it was confident an El Nino weather pattern would exist for the remainder of the year, ABARE said.
ABARE's latest Australian Commodities outlook forecasts that Australia will plant 11.12 million hectares to wheat in 1997/98 against 11.33 million ha the year before.
Australian exports in 1997/98 are forecast at 12.62 million tonnes, down from 18.92 million tonnes the year before.

ABARE said in a note that the latest forecasts were based on a drier than average year but not on the severe drought conditions of 1982/83 and 1994/95 when average wheat yields across Australia were 0.77 and 1.11 tonnes per hectare respectively. Yields in 1997/98 are set at 1.47 tonnes per ha.
Plantings in Australia, Argentina and Canada are forecast to contract, reflecting relatively lower wheat prices compared with other crops, ABARE said.
The U.S. wheat area is estimated to be the lowest in a decade, mainly reflecting increased production flexibility.

World wheat production is forecast to fall by two percent to 569 million tonnes in 1997/98, while consumption is forecast to be marginally down to 576 million tonnes mainly because of substitution by manufacturers of livestock feeds of lower-priced corn for wheat, ABARE said.
World wheat exports were forecast to contract by five percent to 93 million tonnes in 1997/98 as reduced production in many major exporting regions constrains availability.

ABARE forecasts Australia's 1997/98 Australian Standard White (ASW) pool return at A$195.00 a tonne. It also forecasts the world indicator wheat price would average slightly higher in 1997/98 at US$185.00 a tonne against $183.00 in 1996/97.
